cases.question: Are we on pace to hit goal, and where do we land by election day if nothing changes?

facts.name: says we are not on pace

answer.question: Are we on pace to hit goal, and where do we land by election day if nothing changes?
answer.answer:
We're ahead of goal to date (103.3% of the goal-to-date), but if nothing changes we land short of the full goal by about 3,300 doors — roughly 94.6% of the 60,632 total.

- Program doors to date: 33,503 vs goal-to-date 32,431 = 103.3% [table:v_office_pace]
- Projected total by election day: 57,329, which is -3,303 vs the 60,632 goal (94.6%) [table:v_office_pace]
- Northside is the only office over goal: projected 23,583 = 104% (+908) [table:v_office_pace]
- Harbor: projected 19,150 = 95% (-1,007) [table:v_office_pace]
- Eastgate is the biggest gap: projected 14,596 = 82% (-3,204) [table:v_office_pace]
- To close the gap we'd need about 4.1 extra shifts per day program-wide (Eastgate 4.4, Harbor 1.3, Northside 0) [table:v_office_pace]

How it's worked out: the projection assumes nothing changes — doors to date plus the last 7 days' average daily doors (1,489.1) × 16 knocking days left (Oct 19 to Nov 3); an office "will miss goal" when its projection is below its total goal [doc:program-plan#pace-and-projection].

args.query: projection method on pace goal election day

sources.text: Pace compares doors to date with the goal to date. The projection for Election Day assumes nothing changes: doors to date plus the average daily doors of the last 7 days times the knocking days left. An office "will miss goal" when its projection is below its total goal; the shortfall is the goal minus the projection.

cases.question: Based on our pace and what's left, should we ask the client for more doors, or a second pass on the turf we have?

facts.name: doors we can knock in the days left

answer.question: Based on our pace and what's left, should we ask the client for more doors, or a second pass on the turf we have?
answer.answer:
Ask the client for more doors — the program will run out of first-pass turf before Election Day, so new turf is the right ask, with a second pass on not-home doors only as the fallback.

- Program capacity left: 1,489.1 doors/day × 16 days = 23,826 doors [table:v_office_pace]
- First-pass turf left (untouched doors): 10,393 across all offices (Eastgate 1,183, Harbor 8,096, Northside 1,114) [table:v_precinct_coverage]
- Capacity exceeds untouched turf by about 13,433 doors, so we will run out of first-pass turf [table:v_office_pace]
- Not-home doors available for a second pass: 18,555 (Eastgate 4,712, Harbor 6,418, Northside 7,425) [table:v_precinct_coverage]
- The shortfall is concentrated in Eastgate (projected 3,204 doors short) and Harbor (1,007 short); Northside is projected 908 over [table:v_office_pace]

How it's decided: when projected capacity (last 7 days' average daily doors × days left) is larger than the untouched doors left in our turf, we run out of first-pass turf and should ask the client for more doors first, since new turf contacts voters at the normal first-pass rate; a second pass on not-home doors is the fallback because it contacts voters at roughly half the first-pass rate. [doc:program-plan#more-doors-or-a-second-pass]

args.query: more doors or a second pass decision

args.sql: SELECT office, SUM(doors_untouched) AS untouched, SUM(not_home_doors) AS not_home FROM v_precinct_coverage GROUP BY office ORDER BY office

sources.sql: SELECT office, SUM(doors_untouched) AS untouched, SUM(not_home_doors) AS not_home FROM v_precinct_coverage GROUP BY office ORDER BY office

In that case ask the client for more doors first; new turf contacts voters at the normal first-pass rate. A second pass on not-home doors is the fallback, because second passes contact voters at roughly half the first-pass rate. If untouched doors exceed capacity, keep working the turf we have.

cases.question: Why does the client's daily report show more doors than our dashboard for Oct 12?

answer.question: Why does the client's daily report show more doors than our dashboard for Oct 12?
answer.answer:
The client's daily report counts attempts (labeled "doors") pulled at the end of each day before any QC rollback, while our dashboard counts doors with rollbacks removed — so the gap is repeat attempts at the same door plus any attempts later rolled back.

- Eastgate: client reported 498 vs our 342 doors, a gap of 156, driven by 142 rolled-back attempts [table:v_daily_doors] [table:client_daily_report]
- Harbor: client reported 428 vs our 406 doors, a gap of 22 (no rollbacks, so all repeat attempts) [table:v_daily_doors] [table:client_daily_report]
- Northside: client reported 558 vs our 533 doors, a gap of 25 (no rollbacks, so all repeat attempts) [table:v_daily_doors] [table:client_daily_report]
- A normal day shows a gap of a few percent from repeat attempts; a larger gap almost always means a rollback [doc:counting-doors#why-the-client-s-numbers-differ-from-ours]
- Eastgate's much larger gap is the exception, consistent with a rollback that day [doc:counting-doors#why-the-client-s-numbers-differ-from-ours]

How it's worked out: the client's "doors" = attempts before rollback; our doors = attempts minus repeat attempts at the same door and minus rolled-back attempts, so gap = repeat attempts + rolled-back attempts [doc:counting-doors#why-the-client-s-numbers-differ-from-ours].

args.query: why client daily report shows more doors than our dashboard

args.sql: SELECT d.office, d.doors, d.attempts, d.rolled_back_attempts, c.doors_reported, c.doors_reported - d.doors AS gap FROM v_daily_doors d JOIN client_daily_report c ON c.office = d.office AND c.report_date = d.knock_date WHERE d.knock_date = '2026-10-12' ORDER BY d.office

sources.sql: SELECT d.office, d.doors, d.attempts, d.rolled_back_attempts, c.doors_reported, c.doors_reported - d.doors AS gap FROM v_daily_doors d JOIN client_daily_report c ON c.office = d.office AND c.report_date = d.knock_date WHERE d.knock_date = '2026-10-12' ORDER BY d.office

The gap on any day is the repeat attempts at the same door plus any attempts that were later rolled back. A normal day shows a gap of a few percent from repeat attempts. A larger gap almost always means a rollback.

answer.question: Which canvassers had flash knocking or householding flags this week, and is it one person or the whole office?
answer.answer:
This week's flash knocking and householding flags fall on four different people across three offices, so it is not one person or one whole office.

- Dorian Pratt (Eastgate): 3 householding flags (Oct 13, 17, 18) — the only person with more than one [table:v_qc_flags_detail]
- Jalen Ortiz (Eastgate): 1 flash knocking flag (Oct 12), whole shift rolled back [table:v_qc_flags_detail]
- Tomas Reyes (Northside): 1 householding flag (Oct 14) [table:v_qc_flags_detail]
- Priya Nandakumar (Harbor): 1 flash knocking flag (Oct 18) [table:v_qc_flags_detail]
- Eastgate carries 4 of the 5 flags (Pratt x3, Ortiz x1); Northside and Harbor have 1 each [table:v_qc_flags_detail]
- Status: Ortiz and Pratt's Oct 13 flag are reviewed; Pratt's Oct 17–18, Reyes and Nandakumar are still open (need a conversation) [table:v_qc_flags_detail]

So it is spread across individuals in all three offices, with Eastgate and Dorian Pratt accounting for most of them.

cases.question: What counts as flash knocking under our QC rules?

answer.question: What counts as flash knocking under our QC rules?
answer.answer:
Flash knocking is recording doors faster than a person can physically walk to them and knock — specifically, 10 or more consecutive knocks recorded less than 30 seconds apart.

- Trigger: 10+ consecutive knocks each less than 30 seconds apart [doc:qc-rules#flash-knocking]
- Consequence: confirmed flash knocking is rolled back — the knocks in the window no longer count as doors or contacts [doc:qc-rules#flash-knocking]
- A whole shift recorded this way is rolled back in full [doc:qc-rules#flash-knocking]
- Rollbacks happen after the day's client report is pulled, so they never change a report already sent [doc:counting-doors#rollbacks]
- Every open flag needs a conversation between the field lead and the canvasser before the canvasser's next shift [doc:qc-rules#what-happens-after-a-flag]
- Two or more flash knocking flags in one week for the same canvasser go to the field director [doc:qc-rules#what-happens-after-a-flag]

sources.text: Flash knocking is recording doors faster than a person can walk to them and knock. A shift is flagged when 10 or more consecutive knocks are recorded less than 30 seconds apart. Confirmed flash knocking is rolled back: the knocks in the window no longer count as doors or contacts. A whole shift recorded this way is rolled back in full.

When QC confirms flash knocking, the knocks in the flagged window are rolled back: they stay in the data with rolled_back = true but are removed from doors and contacts. Rollbacks happen after the day's client report has been pulled, so they never change a report that was already sent.

Every open flag needs a conversation between the field lead and the canvasser before the canvasser's next shift, using the timestamped evidence on the flag. After the conversation the flag is marked reviewed. Two or more householding or flash knocking flags in one week for the same canvasser go to the field director.

sources.text: Riverbend Votes is a paid GOTV door canvass run from three offices: Northside, Eastgate and Harbor. Knocking started Monday, September 21, 2026 and runs every day through Election Day, Tuesday, November 3, 2026. Each office has its own turf (a list of precincts) and its own daily door goal that ramps up toward Election Day.

Pace compares doors to date with the goal to date. The projection for Election Day assumes nothing changes: doors to date plus the average daily doors of the last 7 days times the knocking days left. An office "will miss goal" when its projection is below its total goal; the shortfall is the goal minus the projection.
